<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document">
<div id="id1" class="ltx_logical-block">
    
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:144%;">Comparative Analysis of LLM Abliteration Methods: A Cross-Architecture Evaluation</span>

<br class="ltx_break"></p>
<p id="p1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">Richard J. Young</p>
<p id="p1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">University of Nevada Las Vegas, Department of Neuroscience</p>
<p id="p1.4" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">ryoung@unlv.edu</p>
</div>
  
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Keywords:</span> abliteration, language models, refusal removal, model editing, representation engineering, LLM safety, safety alignment, jailbreaking</p>
</div>
<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Safety alignment mechanisms in large language models prevent responses to harmful queries through learned refusal behavior, yet these same mechanisms impede legitimate research applications including cognitive modeling, adversarial testing, and security analysis. While abliteration techniques enable surgical removal of refusal representations through directional orthogonalization, the relative effectiveness of available implementations remains uncharacterized.
This study evaluates four abliteration tools (Heretic, DECCP, ErisForge, FailSpy) across sixteen instruction-tuned models (7B–14B parameters), reporting tool compatibility on all 16 models and quantitative metrics on subsets dictated by tool support (Heretic: KL divergence + refusal rate on eight models; benchmark preservation on three models with baselines plus Zephyr-7B-beta).
Single-pass methods demonstrated superior capability preservation on the benchmarked subset (avg GSM8K <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> across three models: ErisForge <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.28" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.28</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.28</annotation></semantics></math> pp; DECCP <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.13" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.13</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.13</annotation></semantics></math> pp), while Bayesian-optimized abliteration produced variable distribution shift (KL divergence: 0.043–1.646) with model-dependent capability impact.
These findings provide researchers with evidence-based selection criteria for abliteration tool deployment across diverse model architectures.
The principal finding indicates that mathematical reasoning capabilities exhibit the highest sensitivity to abliteration interventions, with GSM8K change ranging from <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+1.51" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1.51</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+1.51</annotation></semantics></math> pp to <math id="abstract1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-18.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>18.81</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-18.81</annotation></semantics></math> pp (<math id="abstract1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-26.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>26.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-26.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> relative) depending on tool selection and model architecture.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models deployed for commercial and research applications undergo extensive safety alignment training to refuse potentially harmful requests <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. This alignment serves critical protective functions, preventing misuse for activities including weapons synthesis, social engineering, and the generation of exploitative content. However, the same refusal mechanisms that protect against malicious use impede legitimate research applications. Cognitive science simulations requiring unfiltered behavioral modeling, cybersecurity red-teaming exercises, and studies of model bias and representation all require access to model capabilities that safety alignment deliberately restricts. This creates a fundamental tension between protective alignment and research utility that the field has yet to systematically address.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Prior research has established that refusal behavior in transformer-based language models is mediated by a specific direction in the residual stream activation space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. Arditi et al. demonstrated that this “refusal direction” can be identified by contrasting activations on harmful versus harmless prompts, and that orthogonalizing weight matrices with respect to this direction effectively disables refusal while preserving other capabilities. This technique, termed “abliteration,” has spawned multiple open-source implementations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. Recent theoretical work has extended these findings: Wang et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> demonstrated universality of refusal directions across safety-aligned languages, Piras et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> showed that multi-directional approaches can outperform single-direction ablation, and Wollschläger et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> proposed that refusal may be encoded in concept cones spanning multiple dimensions rather than a single direction. Defensive countermeasures have also emerged, with extended-refusal training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> and representation rerouting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> offering increased resistance to abliteration attacks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the proliferation of abliteration tools and growing theoretical understanding, a critical gap remains: no systematic comparison has characterized the relative effectiveness of available implementations across standardized metrics. Researchers selecting abliteration tools must currently rely on anecdotal reports, tool documentation of varying quality, and trial-and-error experimentation. Critical questions remain unanswered. Which implementation produces the lowest distribution shift from the original model? How do architectural features affect abliteration effectiveness? Do different alignment methodologies yield models with fundamentally different refusal representations? The absence of empirical guidance forces inefficient tool selection and prevents principled understanding of capability-safety tradeoffs across the abliteration landscape.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The present study addresses this gap through a systematic comparative evaluation of four major abliteration tools (Heretic, DECCP, ErisForge, FailSpy) across sixteen instruction-tuned models spanning diverse architectures and alignment methodologies. We separate (i) tool compatibility measured across all 16 models from (ii) quantitative metric comparisons on subsets where tools executed successfully and baseline scores were available. Three hypotheses guide this investigation:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">H1 (Model Dependence)</span>: Abliteration outcomes are strongly model-dependent: under a fixed evaluation protocol, some models will exhibit both low distribution shift (KL divergence) and low remaining refusal rates, while others will exhibit coupled resistance (higher KL divergence and higher residual refusals).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">H2 (Capability Preservation)</span>: On models with complete baselines and multi-tool coverage, single-pass methods (DECCP/ErisForge) will show smaller average capability degradation than optimization-based Heretic, with the largest differences appearing on GSM8K.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">H3 (Alignment Sensitivity, Case Study)</span>: In this sample, the DPO-only model (Zephyr-7B-beta) will show higher abliteration susceptibility (lower remaining refusals) than RLHF-aligned models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">This work contributes (1) a systematic comparative analysis of abliteration tools using standardized metrics, (2) evaluation across diverse architectural features and alignment methodologies, (3) characterization of optimization versus single-pass tradeoffs, and (4) complete reproducibility protocols enabling replication and extension.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background and Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Refusal Direction Theory</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Arditi et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> demonstrated that refusal behavior in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream activation space. This direction can be identified by contrasting activations on harmful versus harmless prompts and computing the mean difference. By projecting weight matrices to be orthogonal to this direction, the model loses its ability to represent, and therefore execute, refusal responses. Recent work has extended this finding, demonstrating that the refusal direction is universal across safety-aligned languages <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> and that multi-directional approaches can outperform single-direction ablation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The mathematical foundation rests on the observation that concepts are represented as linear directions in neural network activation spaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>. Recent theoretical work has challenged the strict single-direction hypothesis, finding that refusal may be encoded in concept cones spanning multiple dimensions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>. Additionally, Zhao et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> showed that LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separate representations, with jailbreaks suppressing refusal without altering internal harmfulness beliefs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Defining the refusal direction as <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\vec{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\vec{r}</annotation></semantics></math>, the abliteration operation for a weight matrix <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> becomes:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{\prime}=W-\alpha\cdot\vec{r}\cdot\vec{r}^{T}\cdot W" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo></mover><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{\prime}=W-\alpha\cdot\vec{r}\cdot\vec{r}^{T}\cdot W</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> controls the ablation strength and <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\vec{r}\cdot\vec{r}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo></mover><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\vec{r}\cdot\vec{r}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> is the projection matrix onto the refusal direction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Ablation Method Variants</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several variants of the basic ablation operation have been developed:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Standard Ablation</span>: The original approach directly subtracts the projection of weights onto the refusal direction. While effective, this can alter the magnitude of weight rows, potentially degrading model capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Norm-Preserving Ablation</span>: Proposed by Lai <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, this method decomposes weight matrices into magnitude and direction components, ablating only the directional component while preserving original row norms.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Projected Ablation</span>: Uses Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization to remove the harmless direction component from the refusal direction before ablation, reducing unintended effects on benign behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Open-Source Abliteration Tools</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Four major open-source implementations have emerged, each with distinct architectural approaches and trade-offs:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Heretic</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> implements Optuna-based Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) parameter optimization, automatically searching across layer ranges, ablation weights, and direction indices to minimize a multi-objective score combining KL divergence and refusal rate. The tool operates directly on PyTorch weight tensors without framework dependencies, enabling universal model compatibility (16/16 models in this evaluation). Processing time ranges from roughly 30–110 minutes per model depending on model size and trial count, with typical configurations using 50 trials to balance exploration and efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FailSpy/abliterator</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> uses TransformerLens hooks for activation caching and direction calculation, enabling interactive exploration of refusal directions across layers. While powerful for interpretability research, TransformerLens model coverage limits compatibility to architectures with explicit support (5/16 models). The tool caches activations from <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>256 harmful/harmless prompt pairs and identifies the layer with maximum refusal direction magnitude for targeted ablation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">llm-abliteration (DECCP)</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite> implements memory-efficient sharded processing with norm-preserving and projected abliteration variants. Originally developed for Chinese LLM censorship removal, the tool processes models in 4-bit quantized shards, dramatically reducing VRAM requirements (<math id="S2.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>8GB vs 16–24GB for full-precision approaches). Single-pass execution completes in approximately 2 minutes (20<math id="S2.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than Heretic), with configurable layer selection based on automatic refusal direction magnitude scanning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ErisForge</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> takes a decoder layer transformation approach, wrapping model layers with custom <span id="S2.SS3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">AblationDecoderLayer</span> or <span id="S2.SS3.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">AdditionDecoderLayer</span> modules that apply direction modifications during forward passes. This architecture enables both refusal removal (ablation) and direction injection (addition), the latter being useful for research applications requiring controlled behavior modification. The tool supports configurable weight parameters (0.6–1.0) controlling ablation strength.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Safety Alignment and Jailbreaking Context</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Modern LLMs undergo multiple stages of safety alignment to prevent generation of harmful content <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>. The typical pipeline begins with <span id="S2.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)</span>, where the pretrained model is trained on curated instruction-response pairs demonstrating appropriate refusal behavior for harmful requests. SFT establishes baseline instruction-following capabilities but may not robustly generalize refusal behavior to novel harmful prompts.
Recent work suggests such safety behaviors can be shallow and brittle, sometimes only a few tokens deep <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> builds on SFT by training a reward model on human preference data comparing response pairs, then optimizing the language model via PPO to maximize this reward while maintaining output quality through KL divergence penalty terms against the SFT model. <span id="S2.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Constitutional AI</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> extends this approach by using the model itself to critique and revise outputs according to a set of principles (the “constitution”), enabling RLAIF (RL from AI Feedback) that reduces reliance on human annotation. <span id="S2.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> reformulates the RLHF objective as a simple classification loss on preference pairs, eliminating the need for explicit reward modeling and significantly simplifying training while achieving comparable alignment quality.
In deployed systems, safety controls often also include separate input/output guardrail models (e.g., Llama Guard) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These alignment techniques embed refusal behavior through gradient updates that modify the model’s internal representations. Critically, the resulting “safety representations” appear to be geometrically localized in activation space, making them susceptible to targeted removal. Mechanistic analyses examine what makes and breaks safety fine-tuning and how safety and capabilities interact <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>. Wei et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> systematically documented failure modes including competing objectives, where models prioritize helpfulness over safety when instructions are sufficiently elaborate. Zou et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> demonstrated that adversarial suffixes discovered through gradient-based optimization transfer across models, suggesting shared vulnerability patterns in alignment training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Standardized benchmarks have emerged to enable systematic evaluation: <span id="S2.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">JailbreakBench</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> provides curated harmful prompts with automated success detection, while <span id="S2.SS4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HarmBench</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> offers a comprehensive framework for evaluating both attack and defense methods across multiple harm categories. These benchmarks contextualize abliteration as one approach among many for bypassing safety measures, distinguished by its white-box requirement (model weight access) but high success rate once applied.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work has proposed defenses against abliteration specifically. Abu Shairah et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> demonstrated that training models on extended-refusal responses distributes the refusal signal across multiple tokens, reducing abliteration effectiveness from 70–80% success to under 10%. Agnihotri et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> showed that refusal-only safety interventions are most fragile to abliteration, while representation rerouting approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> offer more robust protection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The Zephyr model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> provides a particularly relevant case study, as it was trained using DPO without explicit safety considerations. The authors note that “removing the in-built alignment of the datasets boosted performance” but “the model is likely to generate problematic text when prompted.” This design choice makes Zephyr-7B-beta an instructive baseline for evaluating abliteration on models with varying safety training approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methods</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Test Models</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model selection followed a stratified sampling approach designed to capture variance across parameter scale, architectural innovations, training methodology, and geographical origin. Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Test Models ‣ 3 Methods" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> presents the model characteristics.</p>
</div>

<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Evaluation Metrics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Effective abliteration requires balancing two competing objectives: (1) removing refusal behavior to enable responses to previously-refused prompts, and (2) preserving the model’s general capabilities for non-refused tasks. The metric selection in this study addresses both objectives while enabling quantitative comparison across tools.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Abliteration Effectiveness Metrics</span>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">KL Divergence</span>: Abliteration modifies model weights, which can inadvertently alter the probability distribution over tokens even for benign prompts. Kullback-Leibler divergence quantifies this “collateral damage” by measuring how much the abliterated model’s predictions differ from the original. For reference distribution <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> (original) and modified distribution <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> (abliterated):</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="D_{KL}(P\|Q)=\sum_{i}P(i)\log\frac{P(i)}{Q(i)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>log</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{KL}(P\|Q)=\sum_{i}P(i)\log\frac{P(i)}{Q(i)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">First-token prediction divergence is computed on 100 harmless prompts (from <span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mlabonne/harmless_alpaca</span>). Lower KL divergence indicates the abliteration was more surgical, removing refusal while minimally perturbing other behaviors. Values below 0.1 indicate excellent preservation; values above 1.0 suggest significant distribution shift.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Refusal Rate</span>: Measures abliteration success by testing whether the model still refuses harmful requests. The abliterated model is prompted with 100 harmful instructions (from <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mlabonne/harmful_behaviors</span>), and refusals are detected using the marker-based heuristic described below. Lower refusal rates indicate more effective refusal suppression.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attack Success Rate (ASR)</span>: The complement of refusal rate (<math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{ASR}=100\%-\text{Refusal Rate}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>ASR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mtext>Refusal Rate</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{ASR}=100\%-\text{Refusal Rate}</annotation></semantics></math>), representing the percentage of harmful prompts receiving non-refusal responses under the refusal detection heuristic.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Refusal/ASR Validity</span>: Refusal rate is computed using a marker-based heuristic to enable fast evaluation. Responses are normalized (lowercasing, removing emphasis markers, typographic apostrophe normalization, whitespace normalization) and classified as refusals if they contain any of a configurable list of marker substrings (e.g., “sorry”, “i cannot”, “i won’t”, “as an ai”, “illegal”, “unethical”). This approach can produce false positives (responses that mention safety language while still providing actionable content) and false negatives (refusals phrased without the selected markers). We therefore interpret refusal rate and ASR as coarse proxies for refusal suppression rather than ground-truth harmful content generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Capability Preservation Metrics</span>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">A critical concern with abliteration is whether removing the refusal direction degrades general model capabilities. Weight modifications that are too aggressive may impair reasoning, knowledge recall, or language understanding. Capability retention is evaluated using three complementary benchmarks that test distinct cognitive abilities:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MMLU</span> (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>: Tests factual knowledge and reasoning across 57 academic subjects including STEM, humanities, social sciences, and professional domains. MMLU degradation would indicate that abliteration damaged the model’s stored knowledge or retrieval mechanisms. Evaluated in 5-shot format.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GSM8K</span> (Grade School Math) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>: Contains 8.5K grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic reasoning. GSM8K is particularly sensitive to capability degradation because mathematical reasoning requires precise chain-of-thought computation; any perturbation to intermediate representations can cascade into incorrect final answers. Evaluated in 5-shot format with strict answer matching.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HellaSwag</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>: Tests commonsense reasoning by requiring models to select the most plausible continuation of everyday scenarios. HellaSwag measures whether abliteration preserves the model’s understanding of typical event sequences and world knowledge. Evaluated in 10-shot format with normalized accuracy.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">All benchmarks were evaluated using lm-evaluation-harness v0.4.5 with 8-bit quantization for memory efficiency. Results are reported as absolute scores and percentage change from baseline (original model) to isolate abliteration effects from inherent model differences.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Experimental Protocol</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tool Configurations</span>: Each tool was tested with its recommended default configurations to represent typical usage. Heretic used 50 Optuna trials per model with Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) sampling, optimizing for minimal KL divergence subject to refusal rate constraints. DECCP operated in 4-bit quantized mode with sharded processing for memory efficiency. ErisForge used default ablation weights (1.0) with AblationDecoderLayer wrappers. FailSpy/abliterator cached 512 activation samples with TransformerLens hooks on middle layers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hardware Environment</span>: All abliteration experiments were conducted on NVIDIA A100-80GB GPUs (CUDA 12.1) for sufficient VRAM to process 7B–14B parameter models without quantization during abliteration. Benchmark evaluations used NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPUs (16GB) with 8-bit quantization via bitsandbytes for memory efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Software Versions</span>: Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.1.0, Transformers 4.44.0, lm-evaluation-harness 0.4.5, Optuna 3.6.1, TransformerLens 1.14.0. All model weights obtained from Hugging Face Hub with specific revision hashes recorded for reproducibility.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Statistical Analysis</span>: Benchmark scores are reported as mean accuracy percentages. For cross-tool comparisons, percentage point change from baseline (<math id="S3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta=\text{Abliterated}-\text{Baseline}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Abliterated</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>Baseline</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta=\text{Abliterated}-\text{Baseline}</annotation></semantics></math>) is computed to isolate abliteration effects. Effect magnitudes are interpreted as: minimal (<math id="S3.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\Delta|&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\Delta|&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math> pp), moderate (<math id="S3.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\leq|\Delta|&lt;5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\leq|\Delta|&lt;5</annotation></semantics></math> pp), and substantial (<math id="S3.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\Delta|\geq 5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\Delta|\geq 5</annotation></semantics></math> pp). KL divergence values are computed using first-token probability distributions averaged across 100 harmless prompts. Benchmark uncertainty is summarized via standard errors reported by lm-evaluation-harness; Appendix reports 95% confidence intervals computed as score <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\pm 1.96\times\text{stderr}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1.96</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mtext>stderr</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 1.96\times\text{stderr}</annotation></semantics></math>.
<span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Benchmark uncertainty</span>: lm-evaluation-harness reports standard errors for benchmark metrics. In the benchmark runs analyzed here, standard errors were 0.38–0.40 pp for MMLU, 1.23–1.38 pp for GSM8K, and 0.37–0.42 pp for HellaSwag, providing a rough scale for interpreting small differences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reproducibility Measures</span>: All experiments used deterministic CUDA operations where possible. Random seeds were fixed (seed=42) for prompt sampling and model initialization. Complete configuration files, abliterated model weights, and raw benchmark outputs are archived for replication.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Ethical Considerations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This study does not involve human subjects and therefore does not require Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval. All data sources are publicly available: harmful/harmless prompt datasets from Hugging Face (<span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mlabonne/harmful_behaviors</span>, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mlabonne/harmless_alpaca</span>), and pre-trained model weights from public repositories. All abliteration tools evaluated are open-source projects hosted on public GitHub repositories.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dual-Use Considerations</span>: It must be acknowledged that abliteration research occupies dual-use territory, as the same techniques that enable legitimate research applications can potentially facilitate misuse. However, systematic understanding of safety vulnerabilities is <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">prerequisite</span> to building robust protections, not antithetical to them. The history of security research demonstrates repeatedly that obscuring vulnerabilities protects no one: attackers eventually discover flaws independently, while defenders remain blind to what requires protection. Kerckhoffs’s principle in cryptography, which holds that a system should remain secure even when everything except the key is public, applies equally to AI safety. If alignment can be trivially removed by anyone with model weights and a GitHub tutorial, then alignment as currently implemented is not a security mechanism but a speed bump. Understanding <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">why</span> and <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how</span> it fails is the first step toward alignment that cannot be surgically excised.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Specific dual-use concerns are addressed through several considerations:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Prior art and accessibility</span>: All four abliteration tools evaluated in this study were publicly released prior to this research, with extensive documentation, tutorials, and pre-abliterated model weights already available on Hugging Face and GitHub. The techniques characterized in this study (directional orthogonalization, activation caching, layer-wise ablation) are well-documented in blog posts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, academic preprints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, and open-source code. The contribution of this work is systematic evaluation and comparison, not capability advancement. A determined adversary already has unrestricted access to these tools; this research provides no additional capability to such actors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Defensive value</span>: Understanding abliteration vulnerabilities is essential for developing robust safety measures. Recent work has demonstrated that “refusal-only” safety training is particularly susceptible to abliteration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, while representation rerouting approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> and extended-refusal training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> offer more robust protection. This research provides several concrete insights for defenders: (1) The finding that DPO-only models (Zephyr) show highest abliteration susceptibility (98% ASR) while RLHF+DPO models (Llama, Yi) show more resistance suggests that multi-stage alignment creates more distributed safety representations; (2) The dramatic GSM8K sensitivity observed (Yi-1.5-9B: <math id="S3.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-26.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>26.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-26.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> with aggressive ablation) indicates that refusal circuits may overlap with mathematical reasoning, a finding relevant to designing alignment that minimizes “alignment tax” on capabilities; (3) The variance in KL divergence across models (0.043–1.646) reveals that some architectures maintain tighter coupling between safety and general capabilities, informing which models may require fundamentally different alignment approaches.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Legitimate research applications</span>: Uncensored models serve critical research functions that motivated this evaluation: (1) <span id="S3.SS4.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Cognitive science</span>: Simulating unfiltered behavioral responses for psychological modeling without artificial refusal artifacts; (2) <span id="S3.SS4.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Red-teaming and security research</span>: Evaluating downstream system vulnerabilities requires adversarial inputs that safety-aligned models refuse to generate; (3) <span id="S3.SS4.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Bias and fairness auditing</span>: Understanding model representations of sensitive topics requires removing refusal confounds; (4) <span id="S3.SS4.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Creative and literary applications</span>: Fiction involving conflict, violence, or mature themes faces artificial generation barriers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Responsible disclosure</span>: The maintainers of evaluated tools were engaged prior to publication, with benchmark methodology shared and feedback incorporated. No novel vulnerabilities in specific models were discovered that would warrant coordinated disclosure. The evaluation datasets (harmful/harmless prompts) are existing public resources, not novel attack vectors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scope Limitations</span>: This study intentionally excludes: (1) Development or distribution of novel attack techniques beyond existing public methods; (2) Evaluation of abliteration on proprietary/closed-source models (Claude, GPT, Gemini) where such modifications would violate terms of service; (3) Generation or storage of harmful content beyond automated refusal detection keywords; (4) Release of abliterated model weights for models lacking explicit permissive licensing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A Note on Progress</span>: The field of AI safety cannot advance by pretending vulnerabilities do not exist. Every robust security system, from cryptographic protocols to operating system kernels, was built by researchers who first understood how existing systems fail. The same intellectual honesty is required for AI alignment. The finding that current safety training can be surgically removed with minimal capability impact is not an endorsement of doing so; it is a measurement of how far the field must advance. This work contributes to that progress by providing the empirical foundation for building alignment mechanisms that are robust by design rather than by obscurity.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Heretic Abliteration Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Heretic Abliteration Results ‣ 4 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> presents Heretic optimization results for eight representative models (50 Optuna trials per model).</p>
</div>

<tr id="S4.T2.2.10" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T2.2.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" colspan="6">
<span id="S4.T2.2.10.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:432.2pt;">
<span id="S4.T2.2.10.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.T2.2.10.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Refusals are counted on <math id="S4.T2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=100</annotation></semantics></math> harmful prompts using the marker-based heuristic described in Methods.</span></span>
</span></th></tr>
</tfoot>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Key Observations</span>: Zephyr-7B-beta achieved the best balance with only 2/100 refusals and minimal KL divergence (0.076), indicating that DPO-only alignment is particularly amenable to directional ablation. DeepSeek-7B showed excellent capability preservation with the lowest KL divergence (0.043).
Automated cross-validation on UncensorBench generations indicates that the marker heuristic can substantially underestimate ASR on harmful prompts (72.2% vs 95.7% classifier non-refusal across <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=900" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>900</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=900</annotation></semantics></math>), primarily because disclaimer-style answers retain safety language while still responding (Appendix Table <a href="#Sx4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ C. Automated Refusal Heuristic Cross-Validation ‣ Appendix: Additional Uncertainty and Validity Checks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2512.13655v2/fig1_kl_divergence.svg" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:551/341;" width="551" height="341"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Distribution shift (KL divergence) after Heretic abliteration across eight instruction-tuned models. Lower values indicate better preservation of the original token distribution. DeepSeek-7B achieved the lowest divergence (0.043), while Qwen2.5-7B showed the highest (1.646).</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2512.13655v2/fig4_kl_vs_refusal.png" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:583/409;" width="583" height="409" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Abliteration effectiveness trade-off: KL divergence (distribution preservation) vs remaining refusal rate. Models in the lower-left quadrant (e.g., Zephyr-7B, DeepSeek-7B) represent optimal outcomes with minimal distribution shift and effective refusal removal.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Benchmark Preservation Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Benchmark Preservation Results ‣ 4 Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents capability preservation using MMLU, GSM8K, and HellaSwag benchmarks.
Given the reported benchmark standard errors (Methods), small differences (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1 pp) on MMLU and HellaSwag and modest differences on GSM8K should be interpreted cautiously. In contrast, the Yi-1.5-9B GSM8K drop under Heretic (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-18.81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>18.81</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-18.81</annotation></semantics></math> pp) is an order of magnitude larger than the GSM8K standard error, indicating a substantial capability impact rather than sampling noise.</p>
</div>

<td id="S4.T3.2.16.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" colspan="6">
<span id="S4.T3.2.16.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:432.2pt;">
<span id="S4.T3.2.16.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><sup id="S4.T3.2.16.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S4.T3.2.16.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">†</span></sup><span id="S4.T3.2.16.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> Base model benchmark not available; absolute scores shown.</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T3.2.17" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T3.2.17.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" colspan="6">
<span id="S4.T3.2.17.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:432.2pt;">
<span id="S4.T3.2.17.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.T3.2.17.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Benchmarks from lm-evaluation-harness; typical standard errors are <math id="S4.T3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>0.4 pp (MMLU), <math id="S4.T3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1.3 pp (GSM8K), <math id="S4.T3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>0.4 pp (HellaSwag).</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Zephyr-7B Analysis</span>: Zephyr-7B-beta, aligned using DPO-only (no RLHF), showed nearly identical performance between Heretic and DECCP abliteration. Both tools produced similar GSM8K scores (33.36% vs 33.21%), suggesting that the abliteration method has minimal differential impact on DPO-aligned models. The absence of base model benchmarks prevents direct degradation analysis, but the consistent scores across tools indicate stable capability preservation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2512.13655v2/fig6_gsm8k_comparison.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:616/368;" width="616" height="368"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>GSM8K math reasoning comparison across all four benchmarked models. DECCP preserved or improved GSM8K performance relative to Heretic on all models, with the most dramatic difference on Yi-1.5-9B (72.40% vs 52.08%). Zephyr-7B shows nearly identical scores between tools, lacking a base model for reference.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2512.13655v2/fig2_benchmark_heatmap.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:648/409;" width="648" height="409" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Benchmark change heatmap showing percentage change from baseline for each model-tool combination across MMLU, GSM8K, and HellaSwag. Green indicates improvement or minimal degradation; red indicates significant capability loss. Yi-1.5-9B with Heretic shows notable GSM8K degradation (<math id="S4.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-26.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>26.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-26.5\%</annotation></semantics></math>), while DECCP and ErisForge maintain near-baseline performance.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>

<td id="S4.T5.2.12.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">—</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T5.2.13" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T5.2.13.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">Vicuna-7B-v1.5</td>
